teaser: Goliath is missing from this sculpture. Stand in front of it and you find out where he went.
review_notes:
Scipione Borghese fact: confiscation of the Cavalier d'Arpino's paintings (1607, charge of illegal firearms) and the brief jailing of Domenichino: standard accounts, wording simplified.
The statue set aside for the David was Apollo and Daphne.
Photo shows the marble in the Galleria Borghese (match was fulltext, image is the right work).
Carved 1623-24 in about seven months, Bernini aged about 25: from Baldinucci, standard account.
Story that Cardinal Maffeo Barberini held the mirror while Bernini carved his own face: told by Baldinucci and Domenico Bernini, presented as a story.
Original placement against a wall in a ground-floor room of the villa: standard scholarly account.
Height about 170 cm.
Eagle-headed harp read as a nod to the Borghese eagle: usual reading.
Borghese collection sale to Napoleon in 1807 concerned antiquities; the Bernini marbles stayed. State bought the villa in 1902.

lesson.text: The room is in a villa on the edge of Rome, built by Cardinal Scipione Borghese to hold his art and impress his guests. The frescoed walls, the gilded frames and the ancient reliefs you see behind the statue belong to that house. So does the statue. It was carved for this villa in 1623 and 1624 and has never lived anywhere else.

The cardinal was the nephew of a pope and one of the greediest collectors in Europe. His favorite sculptor was a prodigy he had backed since the boy's teens, Gian Lorenzo Bernini, now about 25. Bernini set aside another statue he was carving for the villa and, according to his early biographers, finished this one in seven months.

Scipione Borghese did not always pay for what he wanted. He had one painter's whole collection confiscated over a weapons charge, and had another painter briefly jailed until he agreed to work for him. A large part of the villa's collection was gathered with that kind of pressure.

The subject comes from the Bible. David, a shepherd boy, faces the giant warrior Goliath with nothing but a sling and a few stones. Florence had already produced famous Davids: Donatello showed him after the fight, resting. Michelangelo showed him before it, standing still and thinking. Bernini picked the one moment nobody had carved: the throw itself.
A body about to throw is a wound-up spring. Three lines show how Bernini coils it.

lines.label: The long diagonal
lines.text: From the back foot to the head runs one slanting line. Nothing here is vertical. A figure on a diagonal looks unstable, so your eye expects it to move.

lines.label: The pull back
lines.text: The arm swings across the chest toward the sling. Shoulders turn one way while the hips stay facing the other. That twist is the stored energy.

lines.label: The stretched sling
lines.text: Between the two hands the cords are pulled tight. One hand holds the loaded pouch, the other the ends of the straps. In a second it will all unwind.

lesson.text: Now ask where the stone will go. Not into the marble: there is no giant on the base. David twists toward a target somewhere outside the block, in the room, at about your height. When the statue first stood here it was set close to a wall, so visitors met it from the front and side and walked straight into the line of fire.
Bernini made the space around a statue part of the statue. Goliath is wherever you are standing.

This was new. A Renaissance statue is a closed world, complete inside its outline, and you admire it from outside. A Baroque one, in the style that took over Rome in the 1600s, loves movement, drama and strong feeling, and it reaches out for the viewer. To make that work, the face had to be as tense as the body.

lesson.title: Head and hands
lesson.text: Start at the top, where the effort shows first.

spots.title: The bitten lips
spots.text: The brows are knotted and the lips are sucked in and clamped between the teeth. It is the face of someone straining, not posing. Few statues before this one dared to look so unheroic.

spots.title: Hair in motion
spots.text: The curls are deeply drilled, so shadows gather between them. They look as if the turn of the head had just thrown them sideways.

spots.title: Two hands, one sling
spots.text: The cords are thin strips of marble carved free of the block, with air all around them. A slip of the chisel here would have ruined months of work.

lesson.text: About that face. Bernini's biographers say it is his own, studied in a mirror while he pulled exactly this grimace. They add that the mirror was sometimes held by a friend of the cardinal, Maffeo Barberini. It is a good story, and it may be true: the features match the painted self-portraits of the young Bernini.

In August 1623, while this statue was in progress, Maffeo Barberini was elected pope and took the name Urban VIII. He kept Bernini close for the next twenty years and gave him the biggest job in Rome: filling St. Peter's Basilica with sculpture.

The Bible story has one more detail that Bernini uses. Before the fight, King Saul lends David his own armor. The boy tries it on, finds he cannot move in it, and takes it off. Bernini put that discarded armor in the sculpture, and gave it a practical job as well.
David has thrown off the king's armor. Where did it land?

spots.title: The scaly breastplate
spots.text: It lies behind his front leg, covered in carved scales. It also props up the figure: marble legs alone could not carry a body leaning this far, so the armor works as a hidden support.

lesson.text: Next to the armor, on the base, lies an object that has nothing to do with fighting: a harp. David will later become a king and, by tradition, the poet of the Psalms, the sacred songs of the Bible. The end of the harp is carved as an eagle's head, and the eagle was the emblem of the Borghese family. The patron signed the statue in his own way.

The front foot does not stay on its stage. David's toes curl over the edge of the carved base and grip it, the way a thrower's foot grips the ground. In this photo you can see them at the bottom left, hanging past the rim.

The statue is about 170 cm tall (5 ft 7 in), the height of an ordinary person. Michelangelo's David in Florence is three times that. Bernini did not want a giant on a pedestal. He wanted a young man your own size, in your own room, aiming past your shoulder. Four centuries on, visitors to the villa still step slightly aside.

quiz.question: Which moment of the story did Bernini choose?
options: David standing still before the fight
David in the act of throwing
quiz.explanation: Donatello showed the after, Michelangelo the before, Bernini the throw itself.

quiz.question: Where is Goliath?
options: Outside the statue, where the viewer stands
Carved on the back of the base
quiz.explanation: David aims at a target in the room, which puts the viewer in Goliath's place.

quiz.question: What does the scaly armor behind David's leg also do?
options: It supports the leaning marble figure
quiz.explanation: The discarded breastplate works as a prop for a figure that leans too far for its legs alone.

quiz.question: Whose face is David said to have?
quiz.explanation: Biographers say Bernini studied his own grimace in a mirror.

quiz.question: What does the eagle's head on the harp refer to?
quiz.explanation: The eagle was the emblem of the cardinal's family.

facts.text: Bernini's David was carved for the villa where it still stands today.
facts.explanation: It was made for Cardinal Scipione Borghese's villa in Rome and never left.

facts.text: Bernini's David is taller than Michelangelo's.
facts.explanation: It is about 170 cm tall, a third of the height of Michelangelo's.

facts.text: David's face is calm and relaxed, like a classical hero's.
facts.explanation: His brows are knotted and he bites his lips with effort.
